original_value: Pedestrian trajectory prediction under crowded circumstances is a challenging problem owing to human interaction and the complexity of the trajectory pattern. Various methods have been proposed for solving this problem, ranging from traditional Bayesian analysis to Social Force model and deep learning methods. However, most existing models heavily depend on specific scenarios because the trajectory model is constructed in absolute coordinates even though the motion trajectory as well as human interaction are in relative motion. In this study, a novel trajectory prediction model is proposed to capture the relative motion of pedestrians in extremely crowded scenarios. Trajectory sequences and human interaction are first represented with relative motion and then integrated to our model to predict pedestrians’ trajectories. The proposed model is based on Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) structure and consists of an encoder and a decoder which are trained by truncated back propagation. In addition, an anisotropic neighborhood setting is proposed instead of traditional neighborhood analysis. The proposed approach is validated using trajectory data acquired at an extremely crowded train station in Tokyo, Japan. The trajectory prediction experiments demonstrated that the proposed method outperforms existing methods and is stable for predictions of varying length even when the model is trained with a controlled short trajectory sequence.

result.paraphrase: Predicting pedestrian trajectories in crowded settings is difficult because of human interaction and the complexity of movement patterns. Solutions have ranged from conventional Bayesian analysis to Social Force models and deep learning approaches. Yet most current models are strongly scenario dependent, since they build the trajectory model in absolute coordinates even though both motion trajectories and human interaction are relative. This study proposes a new trajectory prediction model that captures pedestrians’ relative motion in extremely crowded scenes. Trajectory sequences and human interaction are first expressed in relative terms and then incorporated into the model to predict pedestrian paths. The method uses a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) architecture with an encoder and decoder trained by truncated back propagation. It also introduces an anisotropic neighborhood setting instead of standard neighborhood analysis. The approach is evaluated with trajectory data collected at an extremely crowded train station in Tokyo, Japan, and the experiments show that it outperforms existing methods and remains stable across different prediction lengths even when trained on a controlled short trajectory sequence.
